new_statements.quote: The regular accent in Wirangu is on the first syllable of a word, as is the case in all the surrounding languages. It is a fairly heavy stress accent (here marked by ' preceding the stressed syllable). The accent is accompanied by a high pitch intonation. There is a secondary stress on the third syllable of words of more than three syllables (this is here marked by " preceding the syllable that bears the secondary accent). There are however a few situations in which this can vary. In emphatic vocatives and imperatives the accent can shift to the final syllable, which can then show vowel distortion as in: ['wiya] mother ["wi'yai] eh, mother!
new_statements.citation: Hercus, Luise A. 1999. A grammar of the Wirangu language from the west coast of South Australia (Pacific Linguistics C-150). Canberra: ANU. [stress section + discussion of Barngarla-Wirangu relationship]
new_statements.locator: §2.2.2 'Accent and vowel length', (a) 'Accent and pitch', pp. 35-36 (PDF pages 56-57)
new_statements.relation_note: Indirect. The catalog's Parnkalla record (src gordon, antepenultimate stress) is the antepenultimate pattern (identical string to the catalog's Macedonian gordon record), i.e. stress on syllable 2 of 4-syllable words, syllable 3 of 5-syllable words. Hercus's only statement bearing on Parnkalla is that initial accent is 'the case in all the surrounding languages'; initial and antepenultimate coincide for words of 2-3 syllables but differ for 4+ syllables (1000 vs 0100). The book never gives a Parnkalla stress form of its own, so this is an areal generalization by a Thura-Yura specialist, not Parnkalla data.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Wirangu: primary stress on the first syllable of every word, accompanied by high pitch; secondary stress on the third syllable of words longer than three syllables. Hercus states this initial-accent pattern holds 'in all the surrounding languages', which in this book include Parnkalla (named throughout as Wirangu's closest relative and eastern Thura-Yura neighbour, §1.2.3), but the sentence is not a description of Parnkalla data.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the third syllable of words of more than three syllables (Wirangu); in -gardu/-garda derivatives where the main stress moves to the long aa of the suffix, the initial syllable carries a secondary accent (marnaardu ["ma'ɳaaɖu] 'very big', p. 35).
new_statements.exceptions: Emphatic vocatives and imperatives can shift the accent to the final syllable with vowel distortion (["wi'yai] 'eh, mother!'); in words with the emphatic suffix -gardu/-garda the main stress optionally falls on the long a created by elision of the suffix-initial g (marnaardu, gumaardu), or optionally stays initial with high pitch for extreme emphasis (p. 35-36); imperatives show a stronger-than-normal initial stress accent without shift, and the command suffix -ga can be accented and raised in pitch (§5.5.6, pp. 116-118).
new_statements.identity_note: Hercus 1999 is a grammar of Wirangu (wira1265), the Thura-Yura language immediately west of Parnkalla on the west coast of South Australia; it describes Parnkalla only comparatively (§1.2.3 'Parnkalla and Kukata', pp. 10-12, arguing Parnkalla is Wirangu's closest genetic relative) and its stress statement covers Parnkalla only through the phrase 'all the surrounding languages'. Schürmann's Parnkalla was recorded at Port Lincoln in the early 1840s; the O'Grady/Hale 1960 Parnkalla is the speech of Harry Croft, Iron Knob (Middleback Range).

readall_conflicts: The catalog's antepenultimate rule for Parnkalla (src gordon) rests, as far as the material held by the project shows, on Schürmann 1844 (already saved from the 2026-09-16 pass at, printed p. 2, NLA scanned block p019): 'The accentation of words is subject to nearly the same rules as in the English language; dissyllables have the accent on penultima, in words of three or more syllables, it rests on antipenultima; as: kátta, club, márniti, good, wayandata. The latter of these rules however is not observed in the conjugation of verbs which are apt to retain the accent on the first or second syllable of the root, even when followed by more than two syllables; as ngukaintyanna, ngukaintyaranna.' Two later sources disagree with antepenult for longer words: Hercus 1999 (this task) says initial accent holds in Wirangu 'as is the case in all the surrounding languages' (p. 35), and O'Grady 2001 (also held by the project, p. 292, describing Hale's March 1960 Parnkalla and Karlamayi field notes from Harry Croft at Iron Knob) says 'Stress is usually marked and is invariably on the first syllable.' So the 1844 missionary grammar (nouns antepenult, verbs root-initial) stands against a 1960 direct field record (invariably initial) and a 1999 areal generalization (initial); the three agree on 2- and 3-syllable words and differ only on words of four or more syllables (Schürmann's wayándata vs an initial-stress prediction). The Zuckermann 2019 Barngarla revival booklets held by the project sa…

Would let the catalog annotate the StressTyp coder's flag that antepenultimate stress is areally anomalous and that Schuermann's 3-syllable examples (kátta, márniti) are equally consistent with initial stress -- only wayándata and the verb forms discriminate.
